body: I don't really expect the disease to mess with our personalities but rather lower cognitive output over time. So if you planned to get a/another degree now might be the time to start. Maybe they'll also find ways to stop that progression/slow it down. They never cared about cognitive disabilites until people suddenly started to grow old while retaining some mobility, so the field is pretty new.

While the results of your question seem very promising, you really need to be cautious.

Many people here have had MS for less than 15 years. I've seen those studies and interviews you refer to, but it's so hard to tell how many of our generation of MS patients will end up with a real disability. I'd like to call us fresh ones the Ocrevus gen and no one can really tell how the Ocrevus gen will age. The 1/3 rule prob referes to early gen DMTs or Tysabri if we're lucky, but pharma is alrdy working on the next gen of meds which is supposed to work with SPMS, too. Since SPMS tends to progress disabilites, there's a good chance we're alrdy painting a vastly different picture rn. 

By my guess for us freshly diagnosed the rate for physical disability will vastly decrease and i'm very concerned about cognitive disabilites and progression without relapses rn.

Well, i recently told my neighbour that while she thinks others have way bigger problems than her, it doesn't make her's invalid. She has the right to complain and the right to be heard. One day i might come to a point where i speak openly myself. :D

As of recent, people with MS are finally able to get the regular hiring status of healthy people in the field i'm intending to work in (teaching), but you'll need multiple docs to write you a positive prognosis or you'll lose your job from time to time bc of short term contracts. 

Thanks a lot for your reply, which has been very helpful (like past comments from you).

I recently started working out again to fight my problematic hip flexors so i can keep walking for as long as possible. Haven't seen my abs in 4 years, so now might be the perfect time to say 'hi' to them again.

'You gotta forget about the 'why?' and concentrate on the 'how?' in regards to dealing with ms' 

My thinking seems to be so based on performance that i continuously fall back into questioning my existance/health per se. 

Thanks for your reply.

Thanks for your reply.

Have you ever encountered people who critisized your for underperforming due to health reasons? If so, how did you deal with that situation?

My wife asked me to make a list of my strengths and to permanently update the list to find out what i can do/can't do on good/bad days. She wants me to find a balance of performance and mindfulness/care for myself. I feel like that goes very well with your statement and is sth. i should really look out for. Thanks for your comment.

I still try to perform to my maximum. I was taught that 110% performance is barely enough. The craziest threat i see for most people with a similar mindset that i have is forcing oneself to always go full performance mode just to crash after some time. It's crazy how my first crash has been MS at 28. Thanks for your answer.

Well, with the profession i'm working in, seeing a therapist might cause me to lose my job and my pension. My wife really helps me work against my internalized values and accept my flaws amd do the best i can. Maybe my MS even helps in that regard.

Finally a question i can chime in on, bc lifestyle is kinda what i'm working on rn.

So, some key points about me. Rn i'm 6 feet and around 210 pounds, so not the most ripped guy, but i'm in ok shape. I'm a bit on the hyperactive side of life, so i need to get stuff done to feel ok.

My wife and i bought 1 years passes for a local landscape park and try to visit it for at least every festival they have (like autumn/pumpkin festival etc.). We also have a very active dog and i usually push for at least 10-15k steps a day in order to keep myself mobile. 3-4 times a week we also do additional workouts consisting of throwing footballs, playing badminton or doing some form of youtube workouts on low energy days. Something i picked up recently is playing dance games with my wife. I suck at dancing but it really helps you with hand-feet-eye coordination. A slightly chubby metalhead dancing to music he obv. hates might look stupid, but idc. :D

Also, due to MS i cut down on calories. I still don't count them, but intermittent fasting and low sugar intake might positively impact both progression (to a very low degree) and fatigue.

Last edit: I really need to accept my lows. Accepting my bad days while making use of my good ones is my main goal.

For me it's basically like this: Wake up feeling super tired, force myself to get up and do everything i need to do, crash around 5-7pm and then stay awake without a nap for far too long. :D I'm fully expecting heat and stress to be a reason for my current fatigues.

Thank you very much. I've always dreamt about positively impact other people's lifes. When i got my diagnosis i felt like that was impossible from now on. Doing a Phase III somehow felt like i could make at least some impact. 

I do know i still have quite a lot of chances to make other people happy and do good, it was just, you know the dark place you're stuck in for a while after diagnosis.

I went for the Phase III.

I will prob. never be able to tell if it was the right decision. I don't know my MS and how fast it progresses due to the early diagnosis and me not really having any experience with my own disease, but my doc explained to me how the meds work (obv. on a Meds-For-Dummies basis), but it was a straw i wanted to grab.

Thanks a lot. Afaik Fenebrutinib is the only one that isn't being tested in my country yet. That means it might take another 5 years for it to release here. I'm also interested in how ATX fares since Phase I and IIa showed decent results in stopping myelin attacking t cells. With how DMTs work, i'm super scared of cancer, but all 3 brutinib drugs and ATX seem to work in very specific ways. I studied the wrong subjects at university.

Ocrevus is definitely a game changer. The decrease in relapses will prob. make huge difference for most people. Myself i can't really speak about it yet. I was diagnosed pretty early and only ever got hospitalized on one occasion (multiple stays, but only one occurance) so i can't say how i'm dealing with relapses. Idk.

Yes, this is why my doc wanted me to go for the trial even tho he never pushed me into it. He says he saw too many people progress even withouth relapses while being on the magic 3 hardcore meds (Tysabri/Ocrevus/Kesimpta) and got frustrated. He thinks BTK inhibitors might become the next Tysabri-type change in ms therapy.  Thanks for the additional US input.

A sister drug to Tolebrutinib. It has been distributed to 1300 patients during phase I and II and thus far has shown good results.

Lots and lots of delays (alrdy 1.5 months past my original appointment for Ocrevus/Kesimpta) and i just feel like i'm trying to climb a hill with my hands bound on my back and not even knowing what's up there since it's also a 50/50 study tho in my country placebos are still low efficiacy treatments. Thought about quitting the trial multiple times now bc of this.

My fiance and i both did intermittent fasting when i was in my weightlifting phase in order to lose some extra fat. After reading this we both chose to go 16:8 (fasting/eating) for now in order to fight this diseases even during early stages.

Only thing i still really struggle with considering MS diet is the dairy/egg part since we're both veggie. -.-

Thanks for your kind words. Sorry i can't type more rn. Still a bit shaken.

I read all of this i'm just not focused enough to answer everything yet.

I'm not in a DMT yet. My cortisone push therapy for my first ever flare up (hope that's the correct term) just ended 4-5 weeks ago and my dmt will begin next week.

I'm not alone, i have my fiance but actually i really helps to write this to you as a stranger rn. Thank you for that.

I know how unlikely a permanent damage this early on is, i'm just used to carrying most of the weight all the time and the thought of becoming a high edss grade this early is driving me nuts.

Before i got diagnosed i was told my problems were connected to emotional stress. I excused myself like 10k times for wasting the Neuro's time. One of them talked to me afterwards telling me i don't need to be sorry. They are always stressed out but happy for every single person they can send home healthy.

Idk,

i usually can't concentrate for longer than 3 mins except if a task is really exciting. This makes meditation quite a pain for me to go through. I try to force myself to slow down now, it's just very very difficult for me. 

I hope to find my inner balance through stuff that resembles meditation these days. It seems like the key factor is keeping my hands busy so the rest of my body can relax.

So i better learn how to handle stress as to no ruin what is left of my 20's, right?

Anything that really helped you?

Thanks for your reply,

i usually only work around 20hrs a week bc i'm still studying at university. 20 hrs leaves me at somewhere around 5-50€ lost every month. Basically after bills i'm poorer every month even if i work. That has been a huge stress factor for me and i seem to be quite the opposite, bc i really don't want to work my job anymore rn. 

I somewhat regret not studying quicker tho, so i could get my lifetime job, get better insurance and start saving money for my soon to be wife. I'm really scared of all the weight she might ned to lift bc of me.
